statement: In an orchard, three fifths of the trees are apple trees and the rest are pear trees. A storm damages one third of the apple trees and one half of the pear trees. What fraction of all the trees in the orchard is damaged?

choices.misconception: I multiplied one third by one half instead of taking each fraction of its own group of trees.
I took the average of one third and one half, as if there were as many apple trees as pear trees.
I worked out the damaged apple trees correctly but took half of the pear trees to be half of the whole orchard.
I added one third and one half as if both were fractions of the whole orchard.

hints: Each fraction is a fraction of a different group of trees.
Find what fraction of the whole orchard the pear trees are. Then work out the damaged apple trees and the damaged pear trees each as a fraction of the whole orchard, and add.
The pear trees are two fifths of the orchard. One third of three fifths is one fifth.

solutions.reliable: The pear trees are 1 - 3/5 = 2/5 of the orchard. Damaged apple trees: 1/3 of 3/5 = 1/5 of the orchard. Damaged pear trees: 1/2 of 2/5 = 1/5 of the orchard. Together 1/5 + 1/5 = 2/5. The transferable idea: when fractions are taken of different groups, turn each into a fraction of the whole before adding.
solutions.elegant: Pretend there are 15 trees: 9 apple and 6 pear. The storm damages 3 apple trees and 3 pear trees, 6 in all, and 6 out of 15 is 2/5.

whyOnTest: Fractions of different groups test whether you convert each to a fraction of the whole, and the classic slip adds or averages them.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
